chief_complaint: resistant hypertension and flash pulmonary edema
hpi_details: A 59-year-old male presents to the clinic with resistant hypertension and flash pulmonary edema. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: wonders if a blocked blood vessel to his kidney could be causing his blood pressure problems
concerns: He is worried he will wake up choking in the middle of the night again and suffer a fatal heart attack.
expectations: He hopes the doctor will switch him to stronger blood pressure pills and order a chest X-ray to ensure his lungs are clear.

investigation_events.title: Emergency renal function and renovascular assessment
investigation_events.availability_message: Urgent renal function and renal duplex results are now available. Stabilization of flash pulmonary edema must not be delayed while awaiting imaging.

results.value: Hemodynamically significant right renal artery stenosis with elevated peak systolic velocity and a smaller right kidney

clinical_knowledge.topic: Renal Artery Stenosis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Renal Artery Stenosis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes optimized medical therapy (an ACE inhibitor or ARB with close creatinine and potassium monitoring) and reserving renal artery revascularization for selected high-risk presentations such as recurrent flash pulmonary edema, rather than routine stenting, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: resistant hypertension and flash pulmonary edema

Key HPI features: A 59-year-old male presents to the clinic with resistant hypertension and flash pulmonary edema. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 178/104 on three antihypertensive agents (amlodipine, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide). Abdominal bruit auscultated in the epigastrium radiating to the flank; diminished bilateral pedal pulses. Labs: Serum creatinine rose from 1.0 to 1.6 mg/dL after starting lisinopril, potassium 5.0 mEq/L. Renal duplex ultrasound: elevated right renal artery peak systolic velocity with asymmetric kidney size (right kidney smaller), consistent with significant atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Renal Artery Stenosis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Primary hypertension without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Recurrent flash pulmonary edema — a classic clue.
management_principles: Optimize medical therapy for blood pressure and atherosclerotic risk (continue ACE inhibitor/ARB with close creatinine and potassium monitoring, plus a statin and antiplatelet therapy)
Confirm clinically significant stenosis with renal duplex ultrasound or CT/MR angiography, and correlate with the episode of flash pulmonary edema

Reserve renal artery revascularization (stenting) for selected high-risk presentations (recurrent flash pulmonary edema, refractory hypertension despite optimal medical therapy) after specialist review, rather than routine stenting
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: resistant hypertension and flash pulmonary edema

A 59-year-old male presents to the clinic with resistant hypertension and flash pulmonary edema. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 178/104 on three antihypertensive agents (amlodipine, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide). Abdominal bruit auscultated in the epigastrium radiating to the flank; diminished bilateral pedal pulses. Labs: Serum creatinine rose from 1.0 to 1.6 mg/dL after starting lisinopril, potassium 5.0 mEq/L. Renal duplex ultrasound: elevated right renal artery peak systolic velocity with asymmetric kidney size (right kidney smaller), consistent with significant atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis.
reference_soap.assessment: Renal artery stenosis (likely atherosclerotic given age and vascular risk factors) presenting with resistant hypertension and flash pulmonary edema, supported by a rise in creatinine after ACE inhibitor initiation and an abdominal bruit.
reference_soap.plan: Optimize medical therapy for blood pressure and atherosclerotic risk, including an ACE inhibitor or ARB with creatinine and potassium monitoring when appropriate. Confirm clinically significant stenosis with appropriate imaging. Do not routinely stent atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis; consider revascularization with specialist input for selected high-risk presentations such as recurrent flash pulmonary edema.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Renal Artery Stenosis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Renal Artery Stenosis
Implement evidence-based management plan: ACEi/ARB with monitoring of creatinine, renal artery stenting

teaching.one_liner: Narrowing of the renal artery, from atherosclerosis or fibromuscular dysplasia, causes resistant hypertension and recurrent flash pulmonary edema.
red_flags: Recurrent flash pulmonary edema — a classic clue

must_ask.say: How difficult has your blood pressure been to control?
Have you had sudden episodes of severe breathlessness?
Do you have blocked arteries anywhere else, like your legs or heart?
Did your kidney function or blood pressure change after starting an ACE inhibitor?

history.answer: My blood pressure has stayed dangerously high even though I take three blood pressure pills every day, and recently I've had sudden terrifying episodes where I wake up severely short of breath.
The sudden breathing attacks began about two weeks ago, while my blood pressure has been steadily climbing higher over the past two or three months.
During an attack, I feel like I'm suffocating even while sitting completely still, but during the day I can manage light walking around the house.
It hits abruptly out of nowhere, especially in the middle of the night, and takes a few hours to calm down.
Yes, I wake up gasping for air in the middle of the night, and I've had to prop myself up with three pillows just to breathe while lying down.
Lying flat makes the breathlessness much worse right away, but things like dust, cold weather, or moving around don't seem to trigger the attacks.
I notice a wet, noisy bubbling sound in my chest when the attacks happen, but I don't usually wheeze.
During the worst breathing attacks, I cough up a small amount of thin, frothy fluid, but no thick yellow phlegm.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or sweating.
I feel a tight, heavy fullness across my chest when my breathing is at its worst and my pressure spikes, but not a sharp, stabbing pain.
My heart races and thumps hard when I struggle to breathe, but I haven't passed out or felt dizzy.
No, I have never coughed up any blood.
I've noticed some mild puffiness around both ankles by evening, and my scale says I've gained about four pounds over the past two weeks.
No, neither leg is swollen or painful on just one side, and I haven't taken long flights, stayed in bed, or had surgery.
I've been feeling completely drained and worn out over the past few weeks, but I haven't had black tarry stools or bleeding anywhere.
It is very frightening when I can't breathe so I feel panicky, but my fingers and lips don't tingle or go numb.
I have never been diagnosed with asthma, chronic lung disease, or a heart attack, and I don't use any inhalers.
I've worked as an accountant in a quiet office for thirty years, so I haven't been around dust, chemicals, or mold.
No, I don't take any beta-blockers, aspirin, ibuprofen, or heart rhythm drugs.
I've had high blood pressure for five years, but it used to stay around 130 until a few months ago when it suddenly shot above 170.
I've had two sudden nighttime episodes where fluid seemed to rapidly flood my lungs, leaving me gasping and terrified.
I get dull aching and cramps in both calves when I walk briskly for a couple of blocks, and my feet are frequently cold to the touch.
My doctor added lisinopril to my amlodipine and water pill about a month ago, but my blood pressure stayed high, and a routine blood test showed my kidney function worsened.
I read that a narrowed artery feeding blood to the kidney can cause severe blood pressure spikes and lung fluid, and I wonder if that's what is happening to me.
Waking up gasping for air was the scariest moment of my life, and I'm terrified of suffocating in my sleep.
I'm hoping you can give me stronger blood pressure pills and check an X-ray to make sure the fluid is gone.
Other than my high blood pressure diagnosed five years ago, I have no history of diabetes, kidney trouble, or high cholesterol.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I take amlodipine 10 mg, lisinopril 20 mg, and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg every morning without missing a dose, and no over-the-counter pills.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco in my life.
I only have a glass of beer once or twice a month at social gatherings.
I work as an office accountant and live in an apartment with my wife.
My father had high blood pressure and suffered a stroke in his late sixties, but no one in my family had kidney failure.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 178/104 mmHg, heart rate 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and temperature 36.7°C.
Alert and sitting upright with no acute respiratory distress or accessory muscle use at rest; no cyanosis or clubbing.
Mild jugular venous distension noted at 3 cm above the sternal angle at 45 degrees.
Fine end-inspiratory crackles heard at both lung bases bilaterally; no wheezing or rhonchi.
Normal resonant percussion bilaterally without dullness at the lung bases.
Regular rate and rhythm with an audible S4 gallop; no systolic or diastolic murmurs.
Systolic-diastolic vascular bruit auscultated in the epigastrium radiating toward the right flank; active bowel sounds.
Soft, non-tender throughout with no guarding, rigidity, or palpable masses.
No tenderness over either costovertebral angle.
Diminished bilateral dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses (1+ bilaterally); radial and femoral pulses are intact (2+).
Trace 1+ bilateral pitting edema over the pretibial area and ankles.
Calves are symmetric and non-tender bilaterally with no swelling, erythema, or palpable cords.
